Also, consider smoking cessation to prevent further gastrointestinal complications.[patient]: I understand. Thank you, doctor.[doctor]: You're welcome. We’ll take good care of you. Let’s get started right away.[patient]: Okay, thank you.[doctor]: You're welcome. Take care.
Dialogue.401: [doctor] Hello, how are you doing today?[patient] Hi, I'm okay, I guess. I've been having some problems with my digestion, though.[doctor] I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me a bit more about what's been going on?[patient] Sure. For the past 6 weeks, I've been having some issues with my bowel movements. There's been a lot of gas, some occasional lower abdominal pain, and I often feel like I haven't fully emptied my bowels.[doctor] Hmm, I see. How often are these symptoms occurring?[patient] It happens multiple times a day. It's really starting to disrupt my daily routine. I even avoid social gatherings because of it.[doctor] That sounds quite uncomfortable. Have you noticed any other symptoms like fever, weight loss, or changes in your urination?[patient] No, I haven't had any fever or weight loss. My urination seems normal too.[doctor] Okay, that's good to know. Any chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath?[patient] No chest pain or palpitations, and I haven't had any shortness of breath either.[doctor] Alright. What about muscle pain? Have you experienced any of that?[patient] No, no muscle pain.[doctor] Thank you for sharing all that. Let's go over your vital signs quickly. Your blood pressure is 128/76 mmHg, heart rate is 74 bpm, respiratory rate is 16, and your temperature is 98.6°F. Everything looks stable there.[patient] That's good to hear.[doctor] Now, let's move on to a physical exam. I’ll start with your abdomen. Please lie down. [patient] Okay.[doctor] Alright, on inspection, everything looks normal. I’m going to palpate your abdomen now. Let me know if you feel any discomfort.[patient] Sure.[doctor] (Palpating) I can feel some mild tenderness in the lower quadrants. Does it hurt when I press here?[patient] A little bit, yeah.[doctor] Okay, thank you. Now, let me listen to your bowel sounds. (Auscultating) Bowel sounds are present in all four quadrants, which is good. No palpable masses, either.[patient] That’s a relief.[doctor] Based on your symptoms and the physical exam, I have a few thoughts. One possible diagnosis could be Irritable Bowel Syndrome, but we also need to consider other conditions like small intestinal bacterial overgrowth or chronic constipation.[patient] I see. What should I do next?[doctor] First, I’d recommend some dietary modifications. Increasing your fiber intake with more vegetables and whole grains could help improve your symptoms.[patient] Okay, I can do that.[doctor] If we find a bacterial cause, I might prescribe Ciprofloxacin for you. But we'll wait for the test results before starting any medication.[patient] Alright. What tests will you be doing?[doctor] We’ll start with a complete blood count, liver function tests, and electrolytes. We also need to get an abdominal X-ray to rule out any obstructive process.[patient] Got it. When will I know the results?[doctor] We should have the results in about a week. I’d like you to come back in 2 weeks for a review and reassessment.[patient] Okay, that sounds good.[doctor] While we wait for the results, let's discuss some lifestyle changes. Increasing your physical activity can aid digestion, and it’s important to avoid smoking and limit alcohol consumption.[patient] I don’t smoke, but I do have a few beers now and then. I’ll try to cut back.[doctor] Great. Do you have any questions or concerns about the plan?[patient] No, everything sounds clear. I’ll start with the diet changes and wait for the test results.[doctor] Excellent. My nurse will be in shortly to give you the orders for the tests. We’ll see you back in 2 weeks.[patient] Thank you, doctor.[doctor] You’re welcome. Take care and see you soon.[patient] Bye.[doctor] Bye.
Dialogue.402: [doctor]: Hi Mr. Wong, it's good to see you today. How have you been feeling lately?[Mr. Wong]: Hi doctor. I’ve been having a tough time, honestly. My walking and balance have been getting worse over the past year.[doctor]: I see. Can you describe how these symptoms are affecting you?[Mr. Wong]: It’s pretty bad, doctor. It’s moderate to severe. I need to use a cane almost all the time now. It’s really impacting my daily activities.[doctor]: That sounds challenging. Are there any other symptoms you’ve been experiencing?[Mr. Wong]: Yes, I’ve been feeling very tired and fatigued. I also get occasional headaches and sometimes my vision gets blurry.[doctor]: How about your sleep? Are you getting enough rest?[Mr. Wong]: Not really. I manage to get only about 5-6 hours of sleep each night because aches and pains keep waking me up.[doctor]: Hmm, that’s definitely not enough rest. Let’s go through a few more details. Have you noticed any issues with your eyes besides the blurred vision?[Mr. Wong]: Well, I had cataract surgery a few years ago, but other than that, it’s just the occasional blurring.[doctor]: Okay, good to know. How about headaches? How often do you get them?[Mr. Wong]: They’re not very frequent, maybe once or twice a month.[doctor]: Alright. And how would you describe your coordination and balance issues?[Mr. Wong]: My coordination is poor, and I have a lot of trouble balancing. It’s been getting steadily worse.[doctor]: I understand. Any problems with your muscles or joints?[Mr. Wong]: Just the aches and pains that disrupt my sleep. My muscles feel fine otherwise.[doctor]: Got it. Have you had any thyroid issues in the past?[Mr. Wong]: No, not that I know of, but I think we’re waiting on some thyroid function tests, right?[doctor]: Yes, that’s correct. We’ll look into those results when they come in. Now, let’s go over some of your vitals and do a physical examination.[Mr. Wong]: Alright.[doctor]: Your blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, and your pulse is 72 beats per minute. Your respirations are normal at 16 per minute, and your temperature is 98.6°F. Your oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, which is good.[Mr. Wong]: That sounds alright.[doctor]: Now for the physical exam. You’re alert and oriented, but I can see you’re in a bit of distress due to your balance issues. Let’s start with the neurological exam. When you try to touch your nose and then my finger, I notice some dysmetria. Your Romberg test is positive, indicating balance issues.[Mr. Wong]: Yes, I’ve noticed that myself.[doctor]: Your gait is ataxic, meaning it’s unsteady, and you do rely on that cane for walking. Sensation is intact to light touch, pinprick, and vibration in both your arms and legs. Muscle strength is good, 5 out of 5 in all extremities, but there’s increased tone in your lower extremities.[Mr. Wong]: I’ve felt that stiffness too.[doctor]: Your pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light, and there’s no nystagmus. Your heart has a regular rate and rhythm, and I didn’t hear any murmurs. There’s no joint swelling or deformity in your musculoskeletal exam.[Mr. Wong]: That’s a relief.[doctor]: Based on what we’ve discussed and the examination, the primary diagnosis is ataxia, unspecified. However, we need to consider a few possible causes, including multiple sclerosis, cerebellar degeneration, vestibular dysfunction, and thyroid issues.[Mr. Wong]: That sounds like a lot to consider.[doctor]: Yes, but we’ll take it step by step. For now, I’m going to recommend some balance training exercises with a physical therapist to help manage your symptoms.[Mr. Wong]: That sounds good.[doctor]: We’ll also do an MRI of your brain and cervical spine to rule out multiple sclerosis or other demyelinating diseases. Those results should give us more information.[Mr. Wong]: Okay, I understand.[doctor]: Additionally, we’ll check your thyroid function with blood tests to see if there’s any hypo- or hyperthyroidism involved.[Mr. Wong]: Alright.[doctor]: I’m also referring you to an otolaryngologist, Dr. James Lee, to evaluate if there are any vestibular issues contributing to your balance problems.[Mr. Wong]: That makes sense.[doctor]: For your current medications, continue taking your Atorvastatin 20 mg once daily for hyperlipidemia and Lisinopril 10 mg once daily for hypertension.[Mr. Wong]: I will.[doctor]: We’ll schedule a follow-up appointment in 2 months to review your progress and any new test results.[Mr. Wong]: Sounds good.[doctor]: In the meantime, try to maintain a consistent low-fat diet and engage in gentle exercises that don’t require too much walking.[Mr. Wong]: I’ll do my best.[doctor]: I’ve discussed the possible causes of your symptoms and the importance of the planned investigations and referrals. The goal is to rule out serious conditions and find the best way to manage your symptoms.[Mr. Wong]: I appreciate that.[doctor]: The balance training should help improve your quality of life despite your condition. Are there any questions you have at this point?[Mr. Wong]: No, I think you’ve covered everything. I’m just eager to get started on the treatment plan.[doctor]: That’s great to hear. Your motivation is key to making progress. We’ll take this one step at a time.[Mr. Wong]: Thank you, doctor.[doctor]: You’re welcome, Mr. Wong. Take care, and we’ll see you in two months for your follow-up.[Mr. Wong]: Thank you, doctor. I’ll see you then.
Dialogue.403: [doctor]: Good morning, Mr. Lee. How are you feeling today?[patient]: Good morning, doctor. I'm not feeling well. I've been having these severe, throbbing headaches.[doctor]: I see. Hmm, can you tell me more about these headaches? How long have they been going on?[patient]: They've been happening for about two months now. They come about 2-3 times a week.[doctor]: That sounds difficult. Are there any other symptoms that come with these headaches?[patient]: Yes, I get nauseous, and I can't stand bright lights or loud noises when they happen.[doctor]: That must be very uncomfortable. How have these headaches impacted your daily activities?[patient]: They've made it really hard to work. I've had to miss several days because of them.[doctor]: I understand. Are you taking any medications currently?[patient]: Yes, I take fluoxetine 20 mg daily for depression.[doctor]: Alright. How's your sleep? Are you getting enough rest?[patient]: Not really. I usually get around 5-6 hours of sleep per night.[doctor]: Hmm, and how about your meals and physical activity?[patient]: My meal times are pretty irregular, and I don't really exercise regularly.[doctor]: Do you use tobacco or any drugs?[patient]: No, I don't use tobacco or drugs.[doctor]: What about alcohol?[patient]: I drink occasionally, maybe 1-2 drinks per week.[doctor]: Thank you for sharing that. Let’s go over a few more things. Have you experienced any fever, weight loss, or night sweats?[patient]: No, none of those.[doctor]: Any visual disturbances or hearing problems?[patient]: No, my vision and hearing are fine.[doctor]: Are you experiencing any dizziness, weakness, or numbness?[patient]: No, none of that. My nerves feel normal.[doctor]: Thank you. Let me check your vital signs. Your blood pressure is 120/80 mmHg, heart rate is 72 bpm, respiratory rate is 16 breaths per minute, and your temperature is 98.6°F. Everything looks normal there.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: Now let me perform a physical examination. I’m going to check your head for any tenderness.[patient]: Sure.[doctor]: I can feel some tenderness on your temples. Let me also check your eyes, ears, nose, and throat. Everything looks normal there.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: Now, I’ll examine your neurological function. Your cranial nerves seem to be functioning normally, and there are no focal deficits.[patient]: That sounds good.[doctor]: We are awaiting the results of your blood tests, including a complete blood count and a comprehensive metabolic panel, to rule out other potential causes of your headaches.[patient]: Alright.[doctor]: Based on your symptoms and examination, it seems you may be experiencing migraines without aura. Other possibilities include tension-type headaches, cluster headaches, or a secondary headache due to an underlying condition, but we'll wait for the blood test results to confirm.[patient]: What can we do about it?[doctor]: I’m going to prescribe you Sumatriptan 50 mg to take at the onset of a migraine. You can repeat it in 2 hours if needed, but don't exceed 200 mg in 24 hours. I’ll prescribe you 9 tablets.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: I'm also referring you to Dr. Lisa Miller, a psychologist, for cognitive-behavioral therapy to help manage stress and anxiety, which might be contributing to your migraines.[patient]: That sounds helpful.[doctor]: In addition, I recommend you engage in regular physical activity, like at least 30 minutes of aerobic exercise three times a week, improve your sleep hygiene aiming for 7-8 hours of sleep per night, and maintain consistent meal timings with a balanced diet.[patient]: I'll try to do that.[doctor]: We’ll follow up in 3 months to see how the treatment is working for you.[patient]: Alright, I’ll be here.[doctor]: It's important to adhere to the migraine treatment and lifestyle changes we discussed. Reducing the frequency and severity of your migraines will significantly improve your quality of life.[patient]: I understand.[doctor]: Also, considering you live in an urban area with high pollution, try to minimize your exposure to it as much as possible. This could be a contributing factor to your symptoms.[patient]: I'll try my best.[doctor]: Do you have any questions or concerns about the treatment plan?[patient]: No, I think you've covered everything. Thank you, doctor.[doctor]: You're welcome, Mr. Lee. We’re here to support you. If you have any issues or the symptoms worsen, don’t hesitate to contact us.[patient]: I will. Thank you.[doctor]: Take care and see you in three months.[patient]: Thank you, doctor.
Dialogue.404: [doctor] Hi Jane, how are you today?[patient] Hi doctor, I'm doing okay, thank you.[doctor] Great to hear. So, I see this is your initial prenatal visit. How have you been feeling?[patient] Well, I'm 20 weeks along now, and I've been experiencing some mild heartburn daily for the past month and occasional nausea, especially in the mornings. I've also noticed some mild swelling in my feet and I get headaches about once a week.[doctor] Hmm, I see. How have these symptoms affected your daily activities?[patient] The heartburn and nausea make it a bit hard to stand for long periods, and the headaches sometimes make it difficult to concentrate.[doctor] Okay, let’s go over a few things in detail. Have you had any fever, chills, or unexpected weight loss?[patient] No, none of those.[doctor] Alright. How about any vomiting or diarrhea?[patient] No vomiting or diarrhea, just the heartburn and nausea.[doctor] Understood. Any dizziness or visual changes?[patient] No, none of that either.[doctor] And besides the mild swelling in your feet, have you had any joint pain or muscle weakness?[patient] No, no joint pain or muscle weakness.[doctor] Excellent. Now, I see you have a history of anxiety and you're currently taking sertraline 50 mg daily. How has that been working for you?[patient] It’s been working well. I haven’t had any major anxiety issues since I started taking it.[doctor] That’s good to hear. Let's move on to your vitals. Your blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg, which is normal, and your weight is within the normal range for your gestational age. [patient] That's a relief.[doctor] On physical examination, your fundal height is appropriate for 20 weeks and I can hear the fetal heart tones, which is great. There is mild non-pitting edema in both feet, but that's not unusual at this stage.[patient] Okay, that sounds reassuring.[doctor] So, Jane, based on your symptoms and physical examination, it seems like the mild heartburn and occasional nausea are common during pregnancy. The mild swelling in your feet and occasional headaches aren't alarming at this stage either. [patient] That’s good to know.[doctor] Let’s discuss the plan. We’ll schedule regular prenatal visits every two weeks to monitor your pregnancy and address any new or persistent symptoms. We’ll also order an ultrasound to assess fetal growth and check amniotic fluid levels.[patient] Alright.[doctor] For medications, I’m going to prescribe prenatal vitamins with iron and folic acid to support both your health and the baby's development.[patient] Okay.[doctor] To help with the heartburn, try eating smaller, frequent meals, avoid eating before bedtime, and stay away from foods that trigger heartburn for you.[patient] I can do that.[doctor] For the mild swelling, try to elevate your legs whenever possible and consider wearing support stockings.[patient] That makes sense.[doctor] Continue taking your sertraline 50 mg daily for anxiety. It’s important to keep that well-managed.[patient] Will do.[doctor] I also want to emphasize the importance of prenatal yoga and light walking. These activities are beneficial for your physical and mental well-being.[patient] I’ve been trying to keep up with yoga and walking.[doctor] That’s excellent. Also, maintaining good sleep hygiene is important, and try to sleep in a position that reduces heartburn, like on your left side with a pillow to elevate your head and upper body.[patient] I’ll try that. [doctor] Remember to avoid tobacco, alcohol, and any illicit drugs during pregnancy, which I see you’re already doing.[patient] Yes, definitely.[doctor] Continue eating a balanced diet and participating in recreational activities like reading and painting. These contribute to your mental well-being.[patient] I enjoy these activities a lot.[doctor] Wonderful. We’ll schedule an ultrasound appointment and arrange follow-up prenatal visits every two weeks. If you have any concerns or if your symptoms worsen, don’t hesitate to call the clinic.[patient] Thank you, doctor. I appreciate it.[doctor] You’re welcome, Jane. Do you have any other questions or concerns?[patient] No, I think that covers everything for now.[doctor] Great. I’ll have the nurse come in to help schedule your ultrasound and follow-up appointments. Take care, and I’ll see you in two weeks.[patient] Thank you, doctor. See you then.[doctor] Bye, Jane. Take care.
Dialogue.405: [doctor] Hi Ms. Gonzalez, how are you doing today?[patient] Hello doctor, I'm trying my best, but it's been really hard lately.[doctor] I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me more about what's been going on?[patient] Well, I've been having this severe burning pain in both of my feet. It's been getting worse over the past year.[doctor] That sounds very uncomfortable. Is the pain constant or does it come and go?[patient] It's pretty constant. My feet always feel like they're on fire.[doctor] I see. Do you also experience numbness or muscle weakness in your feet?[patient] Yes, both. My feet feel numb, and my muscles are so weak that I can hardly stand or walk without feeling like I'm going to fall.[doctor] That must be very challenging. Have you had any falls recently because of this?[patient] Yes, I've had several falls. It's really affecting my daily activities.[doctor] I'm sorry to hear that. How has this been affecting your sleep?[patient] The pain keeps me up at night. I can't sleep properly, and it's causing insomnia.[doctor] That sounds difficult. Let's go through some of your other health concerns. Do you have any other neurological symptoms besides the burning pain, numbness, and muscle weakness?[patient] No, just those symptoms in my feet.[doctor] Okay. How about your breathing? Have you had any issues with your Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD)?[patient] Yes, I have frequent exacerbations.[doctor] Alright, thank you for sharing that. Let's check your vital signs and do a quick physical exam. Your blood pressure is 130/85 mmHg, your heart rate is 78 beats per minute, your respiratory rate is 18, you are afebrile, and your oxygen saturation is 95% on room air.[patient] Okay, doctor.[doctor] I'm going to listen to your heart now. Your heart rate and rhythm are regular, and I don't hear any murmurs or gallops.[patient] That's good to know.[doctor] Now I'll listen to your lungs. I hear wheezes and decreased breath sounds, which is consistent with your COPD.[patient] Yes, I usually have trouble with my breathing.[doctor] I understand. Let me check your feet. There's a severe loss of sensation, and your muscle strength is decreased in your lower extremities.[patient] That's what I've been feeling.[doctor] Alright, and I don't see any joint swelling or deformities.[patient] That's a relief.[doctor] Based on your symptoms and our examination, it sounds like you have diabetic neuropathy related to your Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus, along with your COPD.[patient] I figured it was related to my diabetes.[doctor] Yes, it often is. For your diabetic neuropathy, I'm going to prescribe Liraglutide 1.2 mg as a daily subcutaneous injection for 90 days and Pregabalin 75 mg to be taken orally twice a day for 30 days.[patient] Will these help with the pain?[doctor] They should help manage your pain and improve your quality of life. We'll follow up in one month to see how you're doing and adjust the Pregabalin if necessary.[patient] Thank you, doctor.[doctor] You're welcome. We also need to manage your diabetes more closely. We'll have a follow-up in three months to assess your diabetes management.[patient] Okay, sounds good.[doctor] I'm also going to refer you to Dr. Alan Brown for an ophthalmology consultation to screen for diabetic retinopathy.[patient] Alright, I'll make sure to follow up with that.[doctor] Additionally, we'll need to do some laboratory tests, including Hemoglobin A1c, Liver Function Tests, and a Complete Blood Count (CBC).[patient] When should I get those done?[doctor] We'll arrange for them to be done as soon as possible.[patient] Okay, I'll get that scheduled.[doctor] For your lifestyle management, I advise maintaining a low-carb diet with regular meal timings. Light physical activities, such as short walks with assistance, can also help as tolerated.[patient] I'll try my best.[doctor] It's also important to manage your sleep hygiene to help with the insomnia caused by your neuropathic pain.[patient] I'll work on that too.[doctor] We'll coordinate with a social worker to address any potential financial constraints you might have that could affect your healthcare access and follow-up visits.[patient] That's very helpful, thank you.[doctor] You're welcome. I have provided some educational materials in Spanish on managing diabetes and preventing complications.[patient] Thank you, that will be very useful.[doctor] We discussed the importance of blood sugar control and adhering to the prescribed treatment regimen.[patient] I understand, doctor. I’ll follow the instructions closely.[doctor] Please report any adverse effects from medications, especially with Pregabalin, and contact the clinic if you have any concerns about your treatment plan.[patient] I will, doctor.[doctor] Regular follow-up appointments are crucial to monitor your condition and adjust the treatment as necessary.[patient] I’ll make sure to come for the follow-ups.[doctor] Great. We’ll see you in one month to assess your pain levels and make any necessary adjustments, and in three months for diabetes management.[patient] Thank you, doctor. I appreciate all your help.[doctor] You're very welcome, Ms. Gonzalez. Take care and see you soon.[patient] Thank you. Goodbye.
Dialogue.406: [doctor]: Good morning, how are you today?[patient]: Good morning, Doctor. I've been better. I'm here because of some severe swelling and pain in my left upper limb.[doctor]: Hmm, I see. Could you tell me more about this swelling and pain? When did it start?[patient]: It started about 4 weeks ago. At first, it wasn't too bad, but it's been getting worse. Now, it's really affecting my ability to do things around the house and even dress myself.[doctor]: I understand. Besides the pain and swelling, have you noticed any other symptoms?[patient]: Yes, there's numbness and tingling in my arm, and sometimes I get these shooting pains. It's really uncomfortable.[doctor]: Okay, and have you had any issues with fatigue or disrupted sleep because of this?[patient]: Definitely. The pain keeps me up at night, and I'm feeling really tired during the day.[doctor]: That sounds very challenging. Let’s go through a quick review of your systems. Have you noticed any other issues with your musculoskeletal system?[patient]: Just the significant pain, swelling, and there's this hard lump in my arm. It feels like it's fixed in place.[doctor]: I see. And neurologically, apart from the numbness and tingling, any other symptoms?[patient]: No, it's just those symptoms in my left arm.[doctor]: Thank you for sharing that. Let's move on to a physical examination. I’ll start by taking your vital signs. Your blood pressure is 140/85 mmHg, heart rate is 78 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 98.6°F, and your oxygen saturation is 97% on room air.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: Now, I’m going to inspect your left upper limb. I can see marked swelling and a hard, fixed mass approximately 4 cm in diameter. There is significant warmth and erythema. Does this hurt when I touch it?[patient]: Yes, it's very tender.[doctor]: I can feel the stiffening of the surrounding muscles. I’m also noticing reduced sensation in the affected area. This doesn’t look reducible.[patient]: What does that mean?[doctor]: It means that the lump doesn’t move or reduce in size when I press on it. We need to consider a few possibilities for this. It could be inflammatory or possibly neoplastic in nature. To get a clearer picture, I’ll refer you to an orthopedic surgeon, Dr. Maria Lopez, for further evaluation and a potential biopsy.[patient]: Oh, okay. That sounds serious.[doctor]: It might be, but it’s important to get a proper diagnosis so we can treat it effectively. In the meantime, I’m going to prescribe you Tramadol 50 mg every 4-6 hours as needed for pain. Here are 30 tablets to start with.[patient]: Alright, thank you.[doctor]: Additionally, I recommend you return to the clinic in one week so we can review the ultrasound and blood work results. Until then, try to keep your arm elevated and apply cold compresses to help manage the swelling.[patient]: I can do that.[doctor]: Also, keep an eye out for any signs of infection, like fever, worsening redness, or discharge. If you notice any of these, seek immediate care.[patient]: Will do. Thank you, Doctor.[doctor]: You’re welcome. Take care and see you next week.[patient]: Thank you, bye.
Dialogue.407: [doctor]: Good morning, Mr. John Doe. How are you feeling today?[patient]: Not good, Doctor. I've got a really bad headache and I can't move my right side properly.[doctor]: Hmm, I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me when this started?[patient]: It started about three hours ago. The headache is really intense, like a 9 out of 10.[doctor]: I see. And have you experienced any nausea or vomiting?[patient]: Yes, I've been feeling nauseous and I've vomited a couple of times.[doctor]: Okay, and have you ever had a headache this severe before?[patient]: No, this is the first time it's been this bad.[doctor]: Alright. Are you able to perform any of your daily activities right now?[patient]: No, I can't do anything. The weakness on my right side is really bad.[doctor]: I understand. Do you have any other symptoms, like fever or chills?[patient]: No, no fever or chills.[doctor]: How about your sleep? How have you been sleeping lately?[patient]: Not great. I usually get around 5 to 6 hours a night.[doctor]: Hmm. And what about your diet and lifestyle? Can you tell me a bit about that?[patient]: I eat a lot of salty foods, and I don't really get much exercise. I smoke a pack of cigarettes a day and drink about 4 to 5 beers a week.[doctor]: Alright. Let's go over some of your medical history. You mentioned you have hypertension. How has that been managed recently?[patient]: It's been controlled with medication until recently. My blood pressure has been high lately.[doctor]: I see. Let's proceed with a physical examination. Your blood pressure is quite high at 185/110 mmHg. Do you feel any chest pain?[patient]: No, no chest pain. Just this horrible headache.[doctor]: Alright, let me check your neurological status. Can you try to lift your right arm and leg for me?[patient]: I can't, Doctor. They're too weak.[doctor]: Okay, that's noted. I'll also check your cardiovascular status. Your blood pressure is indeed elevated. Now, we need to do some tests to determine the cause of your symptoms. We've ordered a CT scan of your head and some blood work, including a complete hematology panel and coagulation profile. We'll also get an MRI of your brain for a detailed evaluation. Does that sound okay?[patient]: Yes, whatever it takes.[doctor]: Great. While we wait for the results, we'll start you on some treatment. We'll give you intravenous Mannitol to help reduce any swelling in your brain. You'll receive 1.5 grams per kilogram as a bolus initially, followed by 0.25 to 0.5 grams per kilogram every 4 to 6 hours.[patient]: Alright.[doctor]: We also need to manage your blood pressure. We'll give you Labetalol, 10 milligrams via IV bolus, and then a continuous infusion at 2 milligrams per minute.[patient]: Okay, Doctor. Will this help with the headache?[doctor]: It should help with the pressure in your head, which might reduce the headache. We'll be closely monitoring you in the ICU and performing neurological checks every 1 to 2 hours.[patient]: What's the next step after this?[doctor]: We'll refer you to a neurosurgeon, Dr. Samantha Lee, for further evaluation and management. She's very experienced and will guide us on the best course of action.[patient]: Alright, Doctor.[doctor]: We also need to get some imaging done immediately. The CT scan of your head should give us an idea of the extent of the hemorrhage. We'll follow up with an MRI for more detailed imaging.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: Additionally, we'll need some blood work, including a complete hematology panel, coagulation profile with PT/INR and aPTT, and liver function tests.[patient]: Got it.[doctor]: Once we have all the results, we'll have a clearer picture of what's going on. In the meantime, I strongly recommend making some lifestyle changes. You'll need to manage your blood pressure through dietary changes, like reducing sodium intake, and cutting down on alcohol.[patient]: I understand. I'll do my best.[doctor]: It's also crucial to quit smoking and increase your physical activity. We'll schedule a follow-up appointment in 4 weeks to reassess your condition.[patient]: I'll try, Doctor.[doctor]: Lastly, I want to educate you on the importance of blood pressure management and adhering to your medication. It's vital for your recovery.[patient]: I understand.[doctor]: Do you have any questions about the treatment plan?[patient]: No, I think I got it all. Thank you, Doctor.[doctor]: You're welcome. We'll take good care of you. I'll be back to check on you soon.[patient]: Thank you.[doctor]: Take care, Mr. Doe. We'll get through this together.[patient]: I appreciate it, Doctor.[doctor]: You're in good hands. We'll start the treatment right away.
Dialogue.408: [doctor] Hello, how are you doing today?[patient] Hello, I am doing okay, thank you.[doctor] I see you’ve come in for a follow-up visit because of a sharp decline in your vision over the past three months. Can you tell me more about that?[patient] Yes, my vision has gotten much worse. I see distortions and have these spots where I can't see anything. It's very hard to read or even recognize faces now.[doctor] I see, that sounds very challenging. Can you describe the visual distortions and these spots you mentioned a bit more?[patient] The lines look wavy and the spots are like dark areas in the center of my vision. It’s there all the time.[doctor] That must be very frustrating. How has this been affecting your daily activities?[patient] It’s very difficult. I can’t read or recognize people’s faces clearly anymore. It’s affecting everything I do.[doctor] I’m sorry to hear that. Let’s go over some other aspects of your health. Have you been sleeping well?[patient] No, not really. My sleep is often interrupted.[doctor] What interrupts your sleep?[patient] I wake up because of low blood sugar at night.[doctor] I see. How is your diabetes management going?[patient] I manage it with insulin, but it’s been hard to control lately.[doctor] Understood. Any other health issues we should know about?[patient] I have Coronary Artery Disease, and I take low-dose aspirin for it.[doctor] How’s your diet been?[patient] It’s mostly carbs. I don’t eat many fruits or vegetables.[doctor] Thank you for sharing that. Now, let’s talk about your ophthalmologic symptoms. You mentioned severe visual distortion and central scotomas. Can you tell me more about when this started?[patient] It started about three months ago and has been getting worse.[doctor] Okay. Let’s also go over your cardiovascular health. You mentioned Coronary Artery Disease. Are you experiencing any chest pain or shortness of breath?[patient] No, I haven’t had any chest pain or shortness of breath.[doctor] That’s good to hear. Let’s proceed with a quick review of your vitals. Your blood pressure is 130/80 mmHg, heart rate is 72 bpm, respiratory rate is 16/min, and temperature is 98.6°F (37°C). I’m going to check your visual acuity.[patient] Okay.[doctor] Your visual acuity tests indicate significant reduction in clarity. Let me perform a dilated fundus examination.[patient] Alright.[doctor] The examination reveals the presence of drusen in both maculas. This is consistent with nonexudative age-related macular degeneration. Let’s also do an Amsler grid test.[patient] Okay.[doctor] The Amsler grid test shows distortion and central scotomas. This confirms what you’ve been experiencing.[patient] Yes, that’s exactly how it looks to me.[doctor] We also performed a Fluorescein Angiography, which shows no neovascularization but confirms the presence of drusen in both maculas. This is consistent with what we’ve seen so far.[patient] I see.[doctor] Based on all these findings, it looks like you have nonexudative age-related macular degeneration. This is a common cause of vision loss in older adults and it’s good that we’ve identified it.[patient] What can I do about it?[doctor] We have several steps we can take. First, I’ll prescribe you the AREDS2 formula vitamins. You’ll need to take one tablet daily. It’s important to take them consistently.[patient] Alright, I’ll try.[doctor] Great. I’ll also refer you to Dr. Morgan Lee, a low vision specialist. He can help you with vision aids and adaptive techniques to manage your daily activities.[patient] That sounds helpful.[doctor] We’ll also schedule a follow-up visit in 6 months to monitor your condition. If there are any changes or concerns before then, please let us know immediately.[patient] Okay, I can do that.[doctor] In terms of lifestyle changes, I recommend increasing your intake of fruits and vegetables. This can help your overall eye health.[patient] It’s hard to get fresh produce where I live.[doctor] I understand. We can look into resources to help you access fresh produce. Additionally, try to incorporate moderate physical activity into your routine. This can improve your overall health.[patient] I’ll do my best.[doctor] Lastly, it’s important to recognize signs that may indicate progression of your condition. If you notice sudden changes in your vision, contact us immediately.[patient] Alright, I’ll watch out for that.[doctor] Also, since you enjoy reading, I recommend looking into audiobooks. They can be a great alternative.[patient] That’s a good idea. I’ll try that.[doctor] Excellent. Do you have any other questions or concerns?[patient] No, I think that covers everything.[doctor] Thank you for your cooperation. We’ll make sure to assist you with accessing fresh produce and safe exercise environments due to your living situation.[patient] Thank you very much.[doctor] You’re welcome. Let’s get those prescriptions and referrals sorted for you. Take care.[patient] Thank you, doctor. Goodbye.[doctor] Goodbye. Take care.
Dialogue.409: [doctor]: Hi, how are you today?[patient]: I've been better, Doctor. I'm really worried about these episodes I've been having.[doctor]: Hmm, I understand. The medical assistant mentioned you're experiencing some transient ischemic attacks, is that correct?[patient]: Yes, that's right. It started about three months ago, and I've had two severe episodes just this past month. It's really scary.[doctor]: I can imagine. Can you describe what happens during these episodes?[patient]: Well, I suddenly feel weak, especially on my right side, and I have trouble speaking. It usually lasts a few minutes, but it's enough to make me worried about doing everyday things.[doctor]: I see. Have these episodes affected your ability to perform routine tasks?[patient]: Yes, definitely. I'm always afraid I'll have another attack, so I avoid doing a lot of things.[doctor]: That must be difficult. Let's talk a bit about your lifestyle. Can you tell me about your diet and physical activity?[patient]: Honestly, my diet isn't great. I eat a lot of fatty foods and high-cholesterol stuff. I don't exercise much either.[doctor]: Okay, and what about smoking and alcohol? Do you smoke or drink?[patient]: I've been smoking a pack a day for 25 years. I also drink socially, maybe 2-3 drinks a week.[doctor]: Alright, thanks for sharing that. It's important for us to get a complete picture. Now, let’s go through a quick review of your systems. Have you experienced any fever, chills, or weight loss?[patient]: No, none of those.[doctor]: How about any chest pain or palpitations?[patient]: No, my heart seems fine.[doctor]: Any issues with your breathing, like shortness of breath or coughing?[patient]: No, my lungs feel okay.[doctor]: Good. How about your gastrointestinal system? Any nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain?[patient]: No problems there either.[doctor]: Any issues with urination, like pain, frequency, or urgency?[patient]: No, everything's normal with that.[doctor]: Alright. And any joint pain or skin issues?[patient]: No joint pain, but I do feel generally weak when I have those episodes. My skin seems fine.[doctor]: Got it. Now, let’s talk about your long-standing Type 2 diabetes. Are you managing it well?[patient]: I try my best, but it's not always easy.[doctor]: Understood. Let's move on to the physical exam now. Your vital signs show a blood pressure of 150/92 on the right arm and 148/90 on the left arm. Your heart rate is 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 18 per minute, and your temperature is 98.4°F. [patient]: Okay, is that normal?[doctor]: Your blood pressure is a bit high, but we’ll address that. Now, let me perform a quick physical examination. [doctor]: (Performs physical exam) You’re alert and oriented, which is good. Your head, eyes, ears, nose, and throat look normal. I did notice a carotid bruit on the left side, which indicates some turbulence in the blood flow.[patient]: What does that mean?[doctor]: It means there might be some narrowing in your carotid artery. Your heart has a regular rate and rhythm, and your lungs are clear. However, during the motor and sensory tests, there was slight weakness on your right side, corresponding to your TIA symptoms.[patient]: That sounds serious.[doctor]: It can be. We also did a duplex ultrasound, which confirmed significant occlusion and stenosis in your left carotid artery, with about 90% stenosis.[patient]: Wow, 90%? That sounds really bad.[doctor]: It is concerning, but we can manage it. We’re awaiting the results of a carotid angiography to plan for surgery. Given your symptoms and the ultrasound findings, I recommend a carotid endarterectomy to alleviate the occlusion and reduce the risk of future TIAs or even a stroke.[patient]: Surgery? That sounds scary.[doctor]: I understand your concern. It's a routine procedure for conditions like yours. We will also start you on aspirin, 81 mg once daily, and atorvastatin, 40 mg once daily, to help manage your cholesterol and prevent clot formation.[patient]: Okay, if that's what you think is best.[doctor]: I do. In addition to the surgery and medications, lifestyle modifications are crucial. We need to get you on a low-cholesterol diet, encourage regular exercise—about 30 minutes of moderate activity daily—and strongly advise smoking cessation. I can refer you to a smoking cessation program.[patient]: I've tried to quit smoking before, but it's really hard.[doctor]: I understand, but it's essential for your health. We can provide support to help you quit. I'll also refer you to a cardiologist to manage your cardiovascular risk factors and possibly a diabetes specialist for better glucose control.[patient]: Alright, I'll do my best.[doctor]: Great. After the surgery, we’ll schedule a follow-up check-up in one week. We’ll also do a follow-up ultrasound of the carotid artery in six months to ensure everything is clear. Do you have any questions about the treatment plan?[patient]: No, I think you covered everything. Just worried about the surgery.[doctor]: It's natural to feel that way, but we'll take good care of you. Remember, this procedure is to prevent further complications. Adhere to the medications and lifestyle changes, and we’ll work together to improve your health.[patient]: Okay, I trust you, Doctor.[doctor]: Thank you. Let's get you scheduled for surgery and start the medications immediately. We’ll also set up your post-operative and cardiologist appointments. Take care, and we'll see you soon for the procedure.[patient]: Alright, thank you, Doctor.[doctor]: You're welcome. See you soon.

I did notice a systolic murmur when I listened to your heart earlier, and you also have some mild peripheral edema. How long have you had the swelling in your legs?[patient] It's been on and off for a few weeks now.[doctor] Okay. I'm going to order an MRI of your brain to rule out any structural abnormalities.[patient] Okay, that sounds good.[doctor] For your medication, I'm going to increase your lamotrigine dose to 150 mg twice daily. I'll prescribe you 60 tablets for a 1-month supply.[patient] Alright, I can do that.[doctor] I'm also referring you to a neuropsychiatrist, Dr. Emma Carter, for cognitive behavioral therapy to help manage your anxiety and stress.[patient] That sounds helpful.[doctor] We'll schedule a follow-up visit in 3 months, but please call immediately if your seizures increase in frequency or severity.[patient] Okay, I will.[doctor] It's very important to adhere to your medication. CBT can significantly help with your anxiety. Please keep a seizure diary to track the frequency, triggers, and characteristics of your auras.[patient] I'll start doing that.[doctor] Also, try to maintain adequate sleep and a balanced diet. Avoid potential seizure triggers like caffeine and alcohol.[patient] I'll make sure to do that.[doctor] Do you have any questions or concerns?[patient] No, I think you've covered everything.[doctor] Great, thank you for coming in today. I hope things improve for you.[patient] Thank you, doctor.[doctor] Take care, and we'll see you in three months.[patient] Sounds good. Thanks again.
Dialogue.416: [doctor] Hi, how are you doing today?[patient] Hi, I'm okay, but I've been having some issues.[doctor] Hmm, I see from the notes that you're experiencing some intermittent sharp abdominal pains. Can you tell me more about that?[patient] Yeah, it's been happening for about a week now. The pain comes and goes multiple times a day and it's really sharp. Sometimes I feel nauseous and I've even vomited a few times.[doctor] That sounds really uncomfortable. How is it affecting your daily life?[patient] It's really hard to focus at work, and I'm a software engineer, so I need to concentrate a lot. It's also interrupting my daily tasks.[doctor] I can understand how that would be disruptive. Have you noticed any changes in your weight or had a fever?[patient] No, my weight hasn't changed and I haven't had a fever.[doctor] Okay, that's good to know. Any headaches or dizziness?[patient] No, I haven't had any headaches or dizziness.[doctor] What about joint or muscle pain?[patient] No, no joint or muscle pain.[doctor] Alright, thank you for sharing all that. Do you have any known allergies?[patient] No, I don't have any allergies.[doctor] And you mentioned you have Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) and you're taking oral contraceptives for it, right?[patient] Yes, that's correct.[doctor] Okay. So, based on your symptoms, I'm suspecting you might have a gastric ulcer. I'll need to order some tests to investigate further. We'll do an abdominal ultrasound and also some blood work including a Complete Blood Count (CBC), Liver function test (LFT), and Pancreatic enzyme levels.[patient] Alright, that sounds good. Will these tests be done soon?[doctor] Yes, we'll arrange for them to be done as soon as possible. In the meantime, I'm going to prescribe you Omeprazole 20 mg, which you should take once daily before meals. I'll give you a 30-day supply.[patient] Okay, I can do that. Is there anything else I should do?[doctor] Yes, I have some lifestyle modifications for you. You should avoid spicy foods, alcohol, and NSAIDs like ibuprofen. Try to follow a bland diet and eat smaller, more frequent meals.[patient] Got it. I'll make sure to follow those instructions.[doctor] Great. I'll also set up a follow-up appointment in 2 weeks via telemedicine to review your symptoms and the ultrasound results. If your symptoms persist after this initial treatment, I will refer you to a gastroenterologist, Dr. Rebecca Lim.[patient] Okay, that sounds like a good plan.[doctor] Finally, it's important for you to monitor your symptoms closely. If you experience severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, or any signs of gastrointestinal bleeding like black stools or vomiting blood, you should seek immediate medical attention.[patient] Understood, I'll keep an eye on those symptoms.[doctor] Excellent. Do you have any questions or concerns at this point?[patient] No, I think you've covered everything. Thank you.[doctor] You're welcome. Take care and we'll talk again in two weeks.[patient] Thank you, I will. Goodbye.[doctor] Goodbye.
Dialogue.417: [doctor]: Good morning, how are you feeling today?[patient]: Not good at all, doctor. I've been feeling really sick for the past few days.[doctor]: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me more about what's been happening?[patient]: Sure. It all started about 5 days ago. I suddenly had this high fever, chills, and a really severe headache. Then I started vomiting and I haven't been able to keep any fluids down.[doctor]: That sounds very uncomfortable. How high has your fever been?[patient]: It's been as high as 39°C. I feel hot and cold at the same time, and my head just keeps pounding.[doctor]: I see. Have you noticed any other symptoms, like a rash or any joint pain or swelling?[patient]: No, no new joint pains or swelling. I have rheumatoid arthritis, so I'm used to some joint pain, but nothing new. And no rashes or anything like that.[doctor]: Okay, that's good to know. Have you been able to eat or drink anything?[patient]: Not really. Every time I try to drink something, I just end up vomiting. My appetite is completely gone, and I've been too weak to get out of bed.[doctor]: That must be very tough. Have you been able to get any sleep?[patient]: Hardly any. The headache and nausea keep waking me up. [doctor]: And you mentioned you have rheumatoid arthritis. Are you currently taking any medication for that?[patient]: Yes, I take methotrexate and prednisone. I've been taking them as prescribed.[doctor]: Okay, thank you for sharing that. I'm going to do a quick physical exam now. Is that alright?[patient]: Yes, that's fine.[doctor]: (Performing physical exam) You appear quite ill and dehydrated. Your temperature is 39°C, blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg, heart rate is 110 bpm, and respiratory rate is 22 bpm. I see you have nuchal rigidity, and both Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are positive. Your heartbeat is rapid but no murmurs or gallops. There's some mild tenderness in your abdomen but no rebound tenderness. No rashes or lesions on your skin.[patient]: What does all that mean, doctor?[doctor]: It means you're showing signs of a serious infection. Based on your symptoms and physical exam, I suspect you might have bacterial meningitis possibly caused by an infection in your bloodstream.[patient]: That sounds serious. What do we do now?[doctor]: We need to start treatment right away. I'm going to prescribe you IV antibiotics: Vancomycin 1g every 12 hours and Ceftriaxone 2g every 12 hours. We'll also give you IV fluids to help with dehydration.[patient]: Okay, and what else do I need to do?[doctor]: We're going to transfer you to a tertiary care hospital for advanced care. We'll need to monitor your blood work, including CBC and renal function tests, on a daily basis. Blood cultures will help us identify the exact cause of the infection. We'll also perform a CT scan of your brain to rule out any complications or abscesses.[patient]: I understand. Will I be okay?[doctor]: We're doing everything we can to make sure you get better. The antibiotics and fluids should help, but it's important for you to be in a hospital where you can get advanced care. [patient]: Thank you, doctor. I'm really scared.[doctor]: I understand, and it's normal to feel anxious. We'll take good care of you. Dr. Sarah Lin, an Infectious Diseases Specialist, will be following up on your case as well. Do you have any other questions or concerns?[patient]: No, I just want to get better.[doctor]: You will. We're here to help you through this. I'll check on you again soon, and the nurse will come in to start your IV antibiotics and fluids.[patient]: Thank you, doctor.[doctor]: You're welcome. We'll get through this together.
Dialogue.418: [doctor]: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. How are you doing today?[patient]: Hi, Dr. Smith. I'm struggling, to be honest. I'm having a really hard time breathing.[doctor]: I'm sorry to hear that. Can you tell me more about your breathing problems?[patient]: It's been really bad. I've had severe shortness of breath for the past four months, and it's just getting worse.[doctor]: Hmm, I see. And do you have any other symptoms along with the shortness of breath?[patient]: Yes, I also have a constant dry cough that won't go away. It's really tiring.[doctor]: I understand. How is your energy level? Are you feeling more fatigued than usual?[patient]: Yes, I'm very fatigued. I feel exhausted all the time, even after a full night's sleep.[doctor]: That sounds very challenging. Have you noticed any swelling in your body, perhaps in your legs or feet?[patient]: Actually, yes. My legs have been swelling up recently. It's making it hard to walk.[doctor]: Alright. Is there anything specific that makes your shortness of breath worse?[patient]: Just about everything. Walking, talking, even just sitting sometimes. It's affecting everything I do.[doctor]: I see. Have you had any chest pain, or have you been coughing up blood?[patient]: No, no chest pain or blood when I cough.[doctor]: How about your appetite or any changes in your bowel or bladder habits?[patient]: No changes there. My appetite is okay, and my bowel and bladder habits are normal.[doctor]: Any joint pain or muscle weakness?[patient]: No, I don't have any joint pain or muscle weakness.[doctor]: What about headaches or dizziness?[patient]: No, I haven't had any headaches or dizziness either.[doctor]: And have you noticed any rashes or skin issues?[patient]: No, my skin seems fine.[doctor]: Alright, thank you for sharing that. Now, let me check your vital signs. Your blood pressure is 128/84 mmHg, heart rate is 98 bpm, respirations are 24 breaths per minute, and your oxygen saturation is 89% on room air.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: I'm going to perform a physical exam now. I'll start by listening to your lungs. Please take a deep breath for me.[patient]: (Takes a deep breath)[doctor]: Hmm, I notice that your breath sounds are diminished bilaterally and you are using your accessory muscles to breathe. Let's move on to your heart. (Listens to heart) Your heart rhythm is regular, and I don't hear any murmurs.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: I'm also seeing some swelling in your lower legs. How long has that been happening?[patient]: It started a few weeks ago and has been getting worse.[doctor]: Alright, let me check your abdomen now. (Palpates abdomen) Your abdomen is soft and non-tender, and I don't feel any enlargement of the liver or spleen.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: Lastly, let's look at your extremities. You have bilateral lower extremity edema, but no cyanosis or clubbing.[patient]: What does that mean?[doctor]: It means there's swelling in both of your legs, but no blue discoloration or abnormal nail growth, which is good.[patient]: Alright.[doctor]: Based on your symptoms and my examination, I'm going to diagnose you with Chronic Respiratory Failure. We'll need to do more tests to determine if it's due to hypoxia or hypercapnia.[patient]: What does that mean?[doctor]: It means your lungs are not effectively exchanging gases, which is why you're feeling short of breath and fatigued. We'll need some more tests to figure out the exact cause.[patient]: Okay, what kind of tests?[doctor]: We'll start with lung function tests, specifically spirometry, to evaluate how well your lungs are working. We'll also need a high-resolution CT scan to assess for interstitial lung disease.[patient]: Alright.[doctor]: In the meantime, I'll initiate continuous home oxygen therapy. You'll need to use 2 liters per minute via a nasal cannula to help improve your oxygen levels.[patient]: Will I have to use it all the time?[doctor]: Yes, it's important to use it continuously to keep your oxygen levels stable.[patient]: Okay, I understand.[doctor]: I'm also prescribing Methylprednisolone, 32 mg daily for 5 days. This will help reduce any inflammation in your lungs.[patient]: Will that help with my breathing?[doctor]: Yes, it should help improve your symptoms.[patient]: Okay.[doctor]: I'm also going to refer you to Dr. Lisa Brown, a nutritionist, to help you develop a dietary plan to improve your overall health.[patient]: That sounds good.[doctor]: Great. We'll also schedule a follow-up appointment in 6 weeks to see how you're doing and review the results of your tests.[patient]: Okay, thank you.[doctor]: I want to emphasize the importance of adhering to the oxygen therapy and medication regimen. If you notice any worsening of symptoms, please seek immediate medical attention.[patient]: I will, thank you.[doctor]: Also, try to engage in low-impact physical activities as tolerated and follow a balanced diet low in carbohydrates and fats. The nutritionist will help you with a tailored plan.[patient]: I'll do my best.[doctor]: Do you have any questions for me?[patient]: No, I think I understand everything.[doctor]: Alright, we'll await the results of the spirometry and high-resolution CT scan. We'll discuss further treatment options based on those results.[patient]: Okay, thank you, doctor.[doctor]: You're welcome. Take care and we'll see you in 6 weeks.[patient]: Thank you. Goodbye.[doctor]: Goodbye.

We'll await those results.[doctor] You're welcome. Do you have any questions or concerns at this time?[parents] Not right now, but we'll reach out if anything comes up.[doctor] Alright, sounds good.
